approach: Teach the subject pronouns as a table, then the bigger lesson for an English speaker: Spanish usually drops them because the verb ending already says who, keeps them for emphasis or contrast, and has no pronoun for "it".
coverage: yo, tú, usted, él, ella, nosotros, nosotras, ustedes, ellos, ellas
tú is informal (friends, family); usted is formal (strangers, elders, clients)
In Latin America ustedes is the plural of both tú and usted
Nosotras and ellas are for all-female groups; nosotros and ellos for male or mixed groups
Spanish usually drops the pronoun: Soy Ana, not Yo soy Ana
A pronoun is kept for emphasis, contrast or clarity: Yo soy de Texas y ella es de Chile
There is no pronoun for "it": Es un libro (It is a book)
tú (you) has an accent; tu (your) does not. él (he) has one; el (the) does not
Recognition only: vosotros (Spain), vos (Argentina, Uruguay, parts of Central America)

data.anchor: Because the verb ending already shows who is acting, Spanish usually leaves out the subject pronoun.
prerequisites: Soy Ana. (I am Ana.) The -oy of soy can only mean "I".
Keep the pronoun for contrast: Yo soy de Texas y él es de Chile.
Keep it for emphasis or to make clear who you mean: Ella es la jefa, no él.
Usted is often kept for politeness: ¿Usted es la señora Ruiz?

blocks.purpose: Targets the reflex of writing yo in front of every verb.

data.question: You are introducing yourself at work. Which sounds most natural?
choices: Él es Marco. Él es ingeniero.
Yo soy Marco. Yo soy ingeniero.

trapReasons.3: English always needs "I", so yo feels required.

data.whyIntuitionFailed: English cannot drop "I", so learners translate it every time.
data.correctReasoning: Soy already means "I am". Repeating yo is grammatical but sounds insistent; Soy Marco. Soy ingeniero. is the natural version.
data.recoveryTip: Use yo only when you are contrasting yourself with someone.

blocks.purpose: Closes with the pronoun set and the dropping habit.

data.takeaway: Learn yo, tú, usted, él, ella, nosotros, ustedes, ellos, ellas, then mostly leave them out: the verb says who, and Spanish has no subject pronoun for "it".

checks.prompt: How do you say "It is a book" in Spanish?
checks.rationale: Spanish has no subject pronoun for a thing, so the verb stands alone: Es un libro. Él and ella mean he and she.
checks.hint: There is no Spanish word for "it" as a subject.

checks.prompt: You are speaking to your two coworkers, Laura and Pedro, in Mexico. Which pronoun means "you" for both of them?
checks.rationale: In Latin America ustedes is the plural you for any group; vosotros is used in Spain, ellos means they and nosotros means we.
checks.hint: Latin America uses one plural you.

checks.prompt: Type the pronoun for "we" when the group is all women.
checks.rationale: Nosotras is we for an all-female group; nosotros is for a male or mixed group.
